title: Design: LRU cache
objective: Build a least-recently-used cache where get and put both take constant time, using a hash map and a doubly linked list together.

sources.title: Python docs: functools.lru_cache (an LRU cache works best when recent calls predict upcoming ones)
Python docs: collections.OrderedDict, suited to implementing LRU caches (move_to_end)

simplifies: The list is drawn singly linked, newest first; the real one also has prev pointers, so a node can be unlinked from the middle in one step. One thread only: a cache shared between threads needs a lock around get and put.

exercise.change: Count cache hits and misses for a dashboard.
exercise.hint: Each service keeps its own dict and order list, with its own copy of the eviction code.

options.text: Write one LRUCache class with get and put, and have each service use its own instance
options.explanation: Right. The caching logic exists once, so counting hits is one edit.

options.text: Add hit counters to each service's copy
options.explanation: Three edits now, and the copies drift apart over time.

options.text: Make the services inherit from each other to share the code
options.explanation: They aren't kinds of each other; composition (each has a cache) fits.

exercise.explain: All three services now use LRUCache. Counting hits and misses is one change inside get(), and every service gets it at once.

quiz.prompt: Why does an LRU cache need both a hash map and a linked list?

options.text: The map finds a key's node in O(1); the list moves and evicts nodes in O(1)
options.explanation: Right. Either one alone makes some operation O(n).
Finding a key in a list means walking it: O(n).
It's a design choice for speed.

quiz.prompt: A cache of 2 holds A (used just now) and B (used earlier). put(C) evicts…

options.explanation: Right. A was used more recently, so B goes.

options.text: A, because it went in first
options.explanation: LRU goes by last use, not by when an item was added.
C is the new item being added.
